subject: Surgery
title: Intestinal Obstruction: Small vs Large Bowel
preview: Bowel obstruction is evaluated with clinical stability, imaging and signs of strangulation rather than an exact symptom-duration formula.

sections.title: Compare small and large bowel patterns
points: Small bowel: prominent vomiting and central dilated loops may occur, with valvulae conniventes crossing the lumen on some radiographs.
Large bowel: greater distension and peripheral haustral patterns may appear; CT often better defines level and cause.

sections.title: Assess danger and treatment direction
points: Evaluate dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, hernia and the possibility of a closed-loop obstruction.
The decision for surgery versus appropriate observation depends on ischemia signs, cause, severity and imaging.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: A plain radiograph does not reliably exclude strangulation or ischemia.
Do not assume every bowel obstruction immediately requires laparotomy, or that persistent worsening signs can safely wait.

quickRevision: Small-bowel obstruction commonly follows adhesions or hernia; large-bowel obstruction has different causes including malignancy and volvulus.
Vomiting, pain, distension and obstipation vary with level, completeness and duration of obstruction.
Peritonitis, escalating continuous pain, fever or physiologic deterioration raise concern for bowel ischemia and require urgent surgical review.

quiz.question: Why are fever, guarding and severe continuous pain concerning in obstruction?
options: They may indicate bowel ischemia or strangulation
quiz.explanation: They may indicate bowel ischemia or strangulation. Strangulation Red Flags (Surgical Emergency): Continuous unremitting pain, fever, tachycardia, localized peritonitis, leukocytosis, and metabolic acidosis (elevated serum lactate).
